data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
inflation_management: The State Bank of Vietnam manages the dong in a crawl against the dollar and has brought inflation down decisively: 23.1% in 2008 and 18.7% in 2011 during the stabilization crisis, then 0.6-4.1% through the late 2010s, 3.2% in 2022, and a projected 3.3% in 2025. The 2011-12 stabilization (tight money, slower credit) was the turning point, establishing credibility that survived the 2022 global shock with only a mild rise. Administered prices (electricity, health) are adjusted in steps, and the central bank has kept the dong's depreciation gradual.
debt_management: Public debt peaked at 47.9% of GDP in 2016 after the 2011-12 banking crisis cleanup and stimulus, then declined steadily to a projected 30.3% in 2025 on rapid growth (GDP from $84.3bn to a projected $494.1bn) and fiscal restraint. Vietnam is rare in having reduced its debt ratio while growing fast. Borrowing is largely domestic and concessional; the 2022 real-estate and bond-market turmoil (notably the Van Thinh Phat/SCB scandal) created contingent risks but did not reach the sovereign balance sheet. The trajectory is among Asia's healthiest.

key_events.event: Inflation hit 23.1% on the commodity boom; stabilization began.
Banking crisis and inflation at 18.7%; decisive tightening restored stability.
Trans-Pacific Partnership signed (later CPTPP after US withdrawal).
CPTPP took effect, boosting trade integration.
COVID-19 contained; Vietnam was among the fastest-growing economies that year.
Anti-corruption 'blazing furnace' campaign intensified; property-bond turmoil hit markets.
Trong died; To Lam consolidated power; manufacturing FDI kept flowing.

outlook_next_decade: Vietnam's base case is 6% growth on FDI-led manufacturing, supply-chain diversification from China, and a young workforce, with low inflation and falling debt. Risks are middle-income transition challenges (productivity, skills), the anti-corruption campaign's chilling effect on administration, US tariff exposure given the large bilateral surplus, and climate vulnerability in the Mekong Delta. Analytical assessment: the macro framework is strong; the question is whether governance keeps pace with the economy's ambitions.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
